Zeitgeist.x: "the general drift of thought or feeling which particularly characterizes any period of time," 1848, from German Zeitgeist (Herder, 1769), "spirit of the age," literally "time-spirit," from Zeit "time" (see tide (n.)) + Geist "spirit" (see ghost (n.)). Carlyle has it 1831 as a German word in "Sartor Resartus."

Zen.x: school of Mahayana Buddhism, by 1727, from Japanese, from Chinese ch'an, ultimately from Sanskrit dhyana "thought, meditation," from PIE root *dheie- "to see, look" (source also of Greek sēma "sign, mark, token;" see semantic). As an adjective from 1881.

Zend.x:
1715, "Parsee sacred book" (in full, Zend-Avesta, more properly Avesta), from Old Persian zend, from Pahlavi zand "commentary," from Avestan zainti- "knowledge," from PIE root *gno- "to know."
Zend was taken to denote the language of the books (formerly Old Bactrian) in 1771 by French scholar Abraham Hyacinthe Anquetil-Duperron. Zend-Avesta is attested in English by 1620s.

Zeus.x: supreme god of the ancient Greeks and master of the others, 1706, from Greek, from PIE *dewos- "god" (source also of Latin deus "god," Old Persian daiva- "demon, evil god," Old Church Slavonic deivai, Sanskrit deva-), from root *dyeu- "to shine," in derivatives "sky, heaven, god." The god-sense is originally "shining," but "whether as originally sun-god or as lightener" is not now clear.

Zoe.x: fem. proper name, Greek, literally "life" (from PIE root *gwei- "to live").

zaftig.x: "alluringly plump, curvaceous, buxom," 1937, from Yiddish zaftik, literally "juicy," from zaft "juice," from Middle High German saft "juice" (see sap (n.1)).

zeal.x:
late 14c., zele, "passionate ardor in pursuit of an objective or course of action," usually desirable (faith, study), but also of wrath or vengeance; from Old French zel (Modern French zèle) and directly from Late Latin zelus "zeal, emulation" (source also of Italian zelo, Spanish celo).
This is a Church word, from Greek zēlos "ardor, eager rivalry, emulation" This was "a noble passion" [Liddell & Scott], but the word also meant "jealousy." It is reconstructed (Watkins) to be from a PIE *ya- "to seek, request, desire."

zealot.x:
early 14c., zelote, member of a militant 1st century Jewish sect which fiercely resisted the Romans in Palestine, from Late Latin zelotes, from Greek zēlōtēs "one who is a zealous follower," from zēloōn "to be zealous," from zēlos "zeal" (see zeal).
The extended sense of "one who is full of zeal" is by 1630s, usually disparaging, "a fanatical enthusiast." Earlier in this sense was zelator, zealer (mid-15c.). Related: Zealotical.

zealous.x:
"full of or incited by zeal" (in the service of a person or cause), 1520s, from Medieval Latin zelosus "full of zeal" (source of Italian zeloso, Spanish celoso), from zelus (see zeal).
The sense of "caused by or manifesting zeal, fervent, inspired" was earlier in English in jealous (late 14c.), which is the same word but through French. Related: Zealously, zealousness. Zealful is attested from c. 1600. Zelotic "of the nature of or characterized by zealotry," is from 1650s; zeloticism is by 1716.

zein.x: simple protein obtained from maize and wheat, 1822, from zea, Late Latin name for "spelt," from Greek zeia "one-seeded wheat, barley, corn" (from PIE root *yewo-) + -in (2).

zenith.x:
"point of the heavens directly overhead at any place," late 14c., zineth, from Old French cenith (Anglo-French zenith, Modern French zénith) and directly from Medieval Latin zyneth, zymeth, cenit, senit, bungled scribal transliterations of Arabic samt "road, path," abbreviation of samt ar-ras, literally "the way over the head." Letter -m- misread as -ni-.
The Medieval Latin word could as well be influenced by the rough agreement of the Arabic term with classical Latin semita "sidetrack, side path" (notion of "thing going off to the side"), from se- "apart" + *mi-ta-, a suffixed form of PIE root *mei- (1) "to change, go, move."
The figurative sense of "highest point or state" of anything capable of having one is from c. 1600. Related: Zenithal.

zeugma.x:
1580s, in prosody and grammar, "a single word made to refer to two or more nouns in a sentence," directly from Greek zeugma, which was used in this secondary sense, primarily "that which is used for joining; a boat a bridge," literally "a yoking," from zeugnynai "to yoke" (reconstructed to be from PIE root *yeug- "to join"). Usually a verb or adjective.
However this might be properly regarded as syllepsis (q.v.). In early use, in Puttenham (1590s), etc., zeugma is introduced as the prosodic term for any verb or adjective made to refer to two or more nouns in a sentence with equal appropriateness. It is thus distinct from syllepsis, in which the word used properly applies only to one of them, as in the Dickens quotes. Puttenham's example of the pure zeugma is
because "Here this word forsooke satisfieth the congruitie and sense of all three clauses ...."

zinc.x:
element, one of the useful metals, 1650s, zinke, from German Zink, perhaps related to Zinke "prong, point;" said to have been used first by Paracelsus (c. 1526) on analogy of the form of its crystals after smelting. Zinke is from Old High German zint "a point, jag."
This is from from Proto-Germanic *teng- "tine" (source also of Old Norse tindr "point, top, summit," Old English tind "prong, spike"), which is reconstructed to be from PIE *denk- "to bite." The spelling with -c- is from 1813, from French influence.

zircon.x:
yellowish mineral occurring in crystal form, 1794, circon, also jargon, a new name given in chemistry to jacinth, from German Zirkon (Klaproth, 1789), which probably is from 18c. French jargon, a vague mineral word used of high-quality diamond-like gemstones.
This has been traced to Medieval Latin jargonce, which is of uncertain origin. Compare Italian giargone, from the same source. Century Dictionary suggests Arabic zarkun "cinnabar." Related: Zirconic; zirconian; zirconate.

zloty.x: monetary unit of Poland, 1842, from Polish złoty, literally "of gold," from złoto "gold," related to Russian zoloto, Czech zlato "gold" (from suffixed form of PIE root *ghel- (2) "to shine;" see gold).

zodiac.x:
"belt of constellations around the ecliptic," within which the planets move, late 14c., zodiak, from Old French zodiaque and directly from Latin zodiacus "zodiac," from Greek zōdiakos (kyklos) "zodiac (circle)," literally "circle of little animals," from zōidion, "sign of the zodiac, sculptured figure of an animal," diminutive of zōion "animal" (from PIE root *gwei- "to live").
Libra is not an animal, but it was not a zodiac constellation to the Greeks, who reckoned 11 but counted Scorpio and its claws (including what is now Libra) as a "double constellation." Libra was figured back in by the Romans.
In Old English the zodiac was twelf tacna "the twelve signs," and in Middle English also Our Ladye's Waye and the Girdle of the Sky.

zoetrope.x: "optical instrument which exhibits pictures as if alive and in action," 1867, literally "wheel of life," from Greek zōē "life" (from PIE root *gwei- "to live") + -trope "that which turns." Related: Zoetropic.

zoic.x: "pertaining to animal life, vital," 1863, in geology, "showing organic remains," from Greek zōikos, "of animals," from zōion "animal" (from PIE root *gwei- "to live").

zollverein.x: 1843, "union of German states for a common tariff," from German Zollverein, literally "customs union," from Zoll "toll" (see toll (n.)) + Verein "union," from vereinen "to unite," from ver- + ein "one" (see one). Later a commercial union generally.

zone.x:
late 14c., "a belt" as an article of dress, also "a belt or band around anything;" from Latin zona "geographical belt, celestial zone," from Greek zōnē "a belt, the girdle worn by women at the hips," from zōnnynai "to gird."
This is reconstructed to be from PIE root *yos- "to gird" (source also of Avestan yasta- "girt," Lithuanian juosiu, juosti "to gird," Old Church Slavonic po-jasu "girdle").
Specifically in geography, one of the five great divisions of the earth's surface (torrid, temperate, frigid; separated by tropics of Cancer and Capricorn and Arctic and Antarctic circles). The 10c. Anglo-Saxon treatise on astronomy translates Latin quinque zonas as fyf gyrdlas.
Extended by c. 1600 to encircling bands generally, and by 1752 to bands or belts of color or shade. The "girdle" sense is obsolete but was preserved in poetry. The meaning "any discrete continuous region distinctly different from adjoining regions" (e.g. demilitarized zone) is recorded by 1822. Zone defense in team sports is recorded from 1927, U.S. football.
1760, "mark with zones," from zone (n.). Land use planning sense is from 1916. Related: Zoned; zoning.

zoning.x: 1819, "a dividing into zones," verbal noun from zone (v.). By 1912 in reference to municipal land-use planning,

zoo.x:
"collection of living animals," by 1866, said to be from 1847 as a colloquial shortening of the name of the Zoological Gardens of the London Zoological Society, which were established 1828 in Regent's Park to house the society's collection of wild animals.
The first three letters were taken but treated as one syllable. "From a mere vulgarism, this corruption has passed into wide colloquial use" [Century Dictionary]. The extended slang meaning "crowded and chaotic place" is recorded by 1935. Zoo-keeper is attested by 1885.

zoolatry.x: also zoolatria, "worship of animals or an animal," attested from 1776, translating French zoolatrtie; see zoo- "animal" + -latry "worship of." Related: Zoolater; zoolatrous.

zoological.x: "of or pertaining to zoology," 1777, from zoology + -ical. Related: Zoolgically.

zoology.x: "the science of animals," 1660s, from Modern Latin zoologia, from Greek zōion "animal" (from PIE root *gwei- "to live") + -logia "study" (see -logy). With botany one of the two main branches of biology.

zoon.x: also zoön, "an animal form containing all elements of a typical organism of its group," 1864 (Herbert Spencer), from Greek zōion "animal" (from PIE root *gwei- "to live"). Related: Zoonic.

zoophilia.x:
"attraction to animals involving release of sexual energy," 1899, in a translation of Krafft-Ebing (it is attested in German by 1894), from zoo- "animal" + -philia.
"[F]ormerly not implying sexual intercourse or bestiality" [OED, 1989], and it was used earlier in 1890s in psychological writing in reference to a morbid sentimentalism over animals. Related: Zoophilic.
Zoophilist is attested by 1829 as "one who has sympathy or tender care for living creatures, opponent of vivisection and animal cruelty;" zoophile in this sense is by 1885, from French. Zoophily is attested by 1886.

zoophobia.x: "morbid or superstitious fear of (certain) animals," 1888, from zoo- "animal" + -phobia. Related: Zoophobic; zoophobe.

zoster.x:
"shingles," 1706, from Latin herpes zoster, from Greek zōstēr "girdle," originally "warrior's belt," from zōnnynai (see zone (n.)).
In Greek antiquity a part of a warrior's gear; in modern use "a belt or girdle, especially for men," by 1824. Earliest in English as kind of seaweed (c. 1600), a sense now obsolete.

zugzwang.x: 1904, in chess, "a forced move that disadvantages the player who must make it," from German Zugzwang, literally "move-compulsion," from Zug "move (in chess); a drawing, pulling, a stretch," from Old High German ziohan "to pull," from Proto-Germanic *teuhan (see tug (v.)).

zwieback.x: 1894, from German Zweiback "biscuit," literally "twice-baked," from zwei "two, twice" (see two) + backen "to bake" (see bake (v.)). A German loan-translation of Italian biscotto (see biscuit).

zygoma.x: "bony arch of the cheek," plural zygomata, 1680s, Modern Latin, from Greek zygōma, from zygon "yoke" (see zygo-). So called because it connects the bones of the face with those of the skull about the ear.

zygomatic.x: in zoology and anatomy, "pertaining to the zygoma," 1709, from Latin zygomaticus, from Greek zygōma (see zygoma).

zygote.x: type of spore formed in reproduction of some fungi and algae, 1880, coined 1878 by German cytologist Eduard Strasburger (1844-1912), the widespread attribution to William Bateson being apparently erroneous; from Greek zygotos "yoked," from zygon "yoke" (see zygo-). Related: Zygotic.

zymurgy.x:
"branch of chemistry which treats of wine-making and brewing," 1868, from Greek zymo-, combining form of zymē "a leaven" (from PIE root *yeue-; see juice) + -ourgia "a working," from ergon "work" (from PIE root *werg- "to do").
It seems to have been a dictionary-word only, before 1900.
It is the last word in many standard English dictionaries (and this one); but Century Dictionary ends with Zyxomma ("A genus of Indian dragon-flies," from Greek zeuxis "a joining") and in the OED [2nd ed.] the last word is zyxt, an obsolete Kentish form of the second person singular of see (v.).

zero.x:
0, the arithmetical figure which stands for nought in the Arabic notation, also "the absence of all quantity considered as quantity," c. 1600, from French zéro or directly from Italian zero, from Medieval Latin zephirum, from Arabic sifr "cipher," a translation of Sanskrit sunya-m "empty place, desert, naught" (see cipher (n.)).
As "initial point of progress or reckoning" in general by 1849, from the point or line on a graduated scale from which reckoning begins (1795). By 1820 as "lowest point or degree" (as in absolute zero). Figuratively, the bottom of any scale.
Abstractly, "nothing, nought," by 1823. The meaning "worthless person or thing, someone who amounts to nothing" is recorded from 1813.
As an adjective from 1810. Zero tolerance is attested by 1972 in U.S. political language. Zero-sum in game theory, indicating that if one player wins X amount the other or others must lose X amount, is from 1944 (von Neumann).
A brief history of the invention of "zero" can be found here.

"aim" (at a target), "set sights" on a target, by 1913, from zero (n.) as "point on a scale where reckoning begins" (by 1795). Hence in rifle-shooting, a method of adjustment using targets at known distances. Related: Zeroed; zeroing. The phrase zero in is by 1944.

Zimbabwe.x: southern African nation, 1980, previously known as Rhodesia (1964-80), renamed upon the end of white rule for a stone-walled city there from medieval times, from Bantu zimba we bahwe "houses of stones," from zimba, plural of imba "house" + bahwe "stones." Zimba, as the name for the 16c. people who inhabited the places, is attested in English by 1901. Related: Zimbabwean.

zip.x: "move rapidly," making a sound expressed by "zip" (see zip (n.1)); by 1852, echoic. Related: Zipped; zipping.

"close or fasten by means of a zip fastener," 1932, back-formation from zipper (n.) or from zip (n.) "zipper." Hence verbal phrase zip up (1959), etc. Related: Zipped; zipping. Zipless is attested by 1973 ("Fear of Flying") in reference to "a brief and passionate sexual encounter" [OED, 1989].

by 1875 as imitative of the sound of something passing rapidly through the air (an insect, a bullet), imitative. By 1900 (paired with zest) as "energy, force impetus."
 Zip gun "homemade pistol" is attested by 1947, U.S., said to be from the sound it makes.
"zero," 1900, student slang for a grade of zero on a test, etc.; of unknown origin; compare zilch. Sometimes used in sports-writing as a transitive verb, "defeat without allowing to score" (by 1976).

Zambia.x: African nation, before independence in 1964 Northern Rhodesia, the new name from the Zambezi River, which is said to be from a local *za "river" also found in the name of Zaire. Related: Zambian.

zombie.x:
also zombi, jumbie, 1788, possibly representing two separate words, one relating to the dead and the other to authority figures, but if so historically these were not kept distinct in English-speaking usage. The oldest attested sense in English is "'spirits of dead wicked men [...] that torment the living.'" The sense of "reanimated corpse" is by 1929, introduced in the work of William Seabrook who observed this sense as a uniquely Haitian concept. The word usually is said to be of West African origin (compare Kikongo zumbi "fetish" and djumbi "ghost"). A sense of "slow-witted person" is recorded from 1936.
It also is attested from 1819 as a title for a chief, in an Afro-Brazilian context. This is said to be directly from the Angolan (Kimbundu) nzambi, "deity." The meaning "witch" is attested by 1910, that of "deity" is by 1921. Grand Zombi as the name of a deity in Voodoo practices is in English by 1904. Zombi was also used as a name for pets in 19c.

zoom.x:
"make a continuous low-pitched buzz or hum; move or travel with or as with a zooming noise;" 1886, of echoic origin.
Picked up by aviators and popularized from c. 1917 as "move quickly toward or past." Also as a noun from 1917, "an act of zooming."
The zoom lens of the photographer and cinematographer is so called by 1932, from the aviation sense. The lens system could change magnification as though "swopping" toward the subject. It was developed by Bell & Howell Co. for motion picture cameras but also was used from the beginning in U.S. Army observation flights.

Zoroastrianism.x: system of religious doctrines taught by Zoroaster, 1854, from Zoroastrian + -ism.

zany.x:
a stock character in old comedies originating on the Italian stage, 1580s, from French zani, from Italian zani, zanni "a zany, clown," originally a proper name, Zanni, the Venetian dialect form of Gianni, pet form of Giovanni "John." Thus the zany is cognate with English Jack.
 He was always slight and thin, well-meaning, but comparatively helpless, full of readiness, grimace, and alacrity, but also of incompetence, eagerly trying to imitate his superior, but ending in failure and absurdity. ["Edinburgh Review," July 1869]
Also by c. 1600, "one who plays the fool for amusement;" other 17c. transferred senses were "follower, assistant; hanger-on, parasite; imitator."
"clownishly imitative; foolish, comically idiotic," 1610s, from zany (n.). Related: Zanily; zaniness.

zephyr.x:
16c. Englishing of Zephirus (late Old English Zefferus), from Latin Zephyrus (source also of French zéphire, Spanish zefiro, Italian zeffiro), from Greek Zephyros, the classical personification of the west wind, mildest and gentlest of the sylvan deities. The word is perhaps related to zophos "the west, the dark region, darkness, gloom."
Extended any soft, mild, gentle breeze by 1610s. Related: Zephyrean; Zephyrous.

Zechariah.x: masc. proper name, Biblical 11th of the Twelve Prophets; see Zachariah.

zucchetto.x:
small, round skull-cap worn by dignitaries in the Catholic Church, 1853, from Italian zucchetta "a cap," originally diminutive of zucca "gourd, head," perhaps from Late Latin cucutia, a word of unknown origin.
Compare zucchini, from a different Italian diminutive of zucca. Properly zucchetta, which is sometimes attested, but the spelling with -o has become established in English.

zooscopy.x: type of hallucination in which imaginary animal forms are perceived, 1889; see zoo- + -scopy. Earlier it meant "zoomancy, divination by observation of animals" (1840). Related: Zooscopic.

zill.x: also zil, zel, "brass finger cymbal used (four at a time) by belly-dancers in certain performances," by 1976, from Turkish zil "cymbal, bell," from Persian zil. Related: Zills.

Zika.x: virus, by 1952, discovered 1947 and named for the Zika Forest of Uganda, where it was first found.

zing.x: 1911, "high pitched sound," of echoic origin. The slang meaning "energy, zest" is attested from 1918. The verb is from 1920; in the meaning "to deliver a stinging witticism or retort" by 1975. Related: Zinged; zinging.

Zion.x: late Old English Sion, from Greek Seon, from Hebrew Tsiyon, name of a Canaanite hill fortress in Jerusalem captured by David and called in the Bible "City of David." It became the center of Jewish life and worship. Related: Zionward (1705), usually figurative, "Heaven-ward."

ziti.x: type of tubular pasta, plural of zita (1845, Eliza Acton), from Italian, said to be a dialect word for "bridegroom."

za.x: U.S. student slang shortening of pizza, attested from 1968.

Zionism.x: 1896, "movement for forming (later supporting) a Jewish national state in Palestine," from German Zionismus (from Zion + Latin-derived suffix -ismus; see -ism); the German word is first attested 1886 in "Selbstemancipation," by "Matthias Acher" (pseudonym of Nathan Birnbaum (1864-1937)).

Zionist.x: 1896, "one who advocates Jewish colonization in Palestine," (also as an adjective); see Zionism + -ist.

Zachariah.x: masc. proper name, Late Latin Zacharias, from Greek Zakharias, from Hebrew Zekharyahu, literally "the Lord has remembered," from zakhar "he remembered." Shortened familiarly to Zack or Zach.

Zanzibar.x: island and former sultanate off East Africa, from Zengi, name of a local people, said to mean "black," + Arabic barr "coast, shore." Related: Zanzibari.

Zwinglian.x: 1532, with -ian + name of Ulrich Zwingli (1484-1531), Swiss Protestant reformer who revolted from the Roman communion in 1516 but who differed from Luther on theological points relating to the real presence in the Eucharist.

zoanthropy.x: form of insanity in which a man imagines himself to be another type of beast, 1845, from French zoanthrope or directly from Modern Latin zoanthropia, from Greek zoion "animal" (from PIE root *gwei- "to live") + anthrōpos "man" (see anthropo-). Compare lycanthropy.

zonk.x: 1950, "to hit hard;" 1968, "put into a stupor;" slang term, of echoic origin (it is attested by 1949 as the sound of a blow). Zonked is by 1959 as "intoxicated," 1972 as "tired out."

zori.x: 1823, from Japanese zori, from so "grass, (rice) straw" + ri "footwear, sole."

zouk.x: Creole French, "party," from zouker "engage in unrestrained social activity."

zoography.x: "descriptive zoology; a treatise on animals," 1590s, from zoo- "animal" + -graphy. Related: Zoographer; zoographist; zoographic; zoographical.

zootheism.x:
"attribution of deity to animals; animal forms as objects of worship," 1879 (John Wesley Powell); see zoo- + -theism. Related: Zootheistic.
 In Norse mythology, we have Fenris the wolf, and Jormungandur the serpent. Dragons appear in Greek mythology, the bull is an Egyptian god, a serpent is found in the Zendavesta; and was there not a scaly fellow in the garden of Eden? So common are these beast-demons in the higher mythologies that they are used in every literature as a rhetorical figure. [Powell, "Mythologic Philosophy," Popular Science, October 1879]

Zoroastrian.x: 1743, "of or pertaining to Zoroaster," founder of the ancient Persian religion, from Latin Zoroastres, from Old Persian Zarathushtra, 6c. or 7c. B.C.E. Persian religious teacher. The name appears to be literally "whose camels are old," from *zarant "old" (cognate with Greek geron, genitive gerontos "old;" see gerontology) + ushtra "camel." As a noun, "a follower of Zoroaster," by 1811.

Zuni.x: native people and language of New Mexico, 1834, from Spanish, from a local native word.

Zulu.x: one of a Bantu people of South Africa, 1824, a native name. As radio code word for -z- from 1960.

Zohar.x: Jewish mystical commentary on the Pentateuch, 1680s, Hebrew, literally "light, splendor."

zig-zag.x:
also zigzag, 1712, "series of short lines angled alternately," like a lightning bolt; "something characterized by such a form;" from French zigzag (1670s), which is perhaps from German Zickzack (though this is attested only from 1703), possibly a reduplication of Zacke "tooth, prong."
The earliest use in German is in reference to military siege approaches. Originally in English it was used to describe the layout of certain garden paths. As "a sharp turning back and forth or in and out," by 1728.
As an adjective from 1750; the verb, "have a zig-zag course or direction," is recorded from 1774. The brand of cigarette paper is from 1909. Related: Zig-zagged; zig-zagging; zig-zaggey.

zoo-.x: word-forming element meaning "animal, living being," from Greek zōion "an animal," literally "a living being," related to zōē "animal life, organic life;" reconstructed to be from PIE root *gwei- "to live," source also of Greek bios "life;" compare bio-.

Zyklon.x:
type of fumigant used to kill rats in enclosed spaces (holds of ships, boxcars, etc.), 1926, from German Zyklon, commercial name of a type of hydrogen cyanide, said to be of unknown etymology, but it is the usual German form of the word cyclone.
There were at least three varieties, A, B, and C, Zyklon-B being the one notoriously used in the Nazi death camps. Zyklon-B also was the name of the process of extermination, involving atomizers and sprayers, that released the chemical product, marketed overseas. It was tested in Britain in 1926 and in use in some U.S. ports by 1927.
 Under direction of Maj. H.A. Spencer of the U.S. public health service, the tanker China Arrow was fumigated yesterday with the new Zyklon-B powder, instead of cyanide. The experiment was the first held at the port with the new mixture, which is reported to be more powerful, efficient, easier to handle and not so dangerous as cyanide. [Los Angeles Daily News, Jan. 6, 1927]
Insect exterminators in Australia advertised use of Zykon-B by 1929. Its use in Nazi death camps began to be noted in U.S. press in 1946.

zoned.x:
1718, in poetry, "wearing a girdle," hence "chaste," from zone (n.) in its original sense. By 1794 as "having zones or bands." In reference to municipal land-use planning maps, by 1920.
As "in a state of drug-induced euphoria" by 1969, from ozone (n.), which is found high in the atmosphere (compare space (v.)); the related verb zone is attested by 1980s.

Ziegfeld.x: in reference to showgirls or stage revues, by 1909, from Florenz Ziegfeld Jr. (1869-1932), U.S. theatrical producer, who staged annual "follies" from 1907-1931. Ziegfeld girl is by 1909, in full Ziegfeld Beauty Girl.

Zingaro.x: a Gypsy, 1580s, from the Italian word, which is of unknown origin (see Gypsy).

ziphoid.x: 1870, in zoology, "resembling or related to Ziphius," a genus of toothed whales (Cuvier, 1834), Modern Latin, from Greek Greek xiphias "swordfish" (see xiphoid).

zag.x: "move in a direction inclined at an angle to that indicated by 'zig,' " 1793, from zig-zag (q.v.).

zap.x: 1929 as a sound, 1942 as a verb; a science-fiction comic strip word (especially from "Buck Rogers in the Twenty-Fifth Century"), imitative of the supposed sound made by a ray-weapon. The verb is by 1942 as "kill, do away with." The meaning "erase electronically" is attested by 1982. Related: Zapped; zapping.

zed.x:
"the name of the letter Z in the alphabet," late 12c., probably from Old French zede, from Late Latin zeta, from Greek zēta, from Hebrew zayin, letter name, literally "weapon;" so called in reference to the shape of this letter in ancient Hebrew. U.S. pronunciation zee is attested by 1670s.
 Of z Dr. Webster says : "It is pronounced zee." So he has taught Americans to call it ; but this fact did not warrant him in stating roundly what he knew to be, with regard to all Britons, totally false. [Fitzedward Hall, "Modern English," 1873]
Other dialectal names for the letter are izzard, ezod, uzzard, and zod. A variant zad developed a colloquial extended sense of "crooked-shaped person or thing" (1725).
 ZEDLAND. Great part of the west country, where the letter Z is substituted for S ; as zee for see, zun for sun, &c. &c. This prevails through the counties of Devonshire, Dorsetshire, and Somersetshire. [Grose, 1796]

zee.x: "the letter Z," 1670s, now more common in American English; see zed.

zek.x: "Russian condemned person in a prison or labor camp," 1968, from Russian zek, probably representing a vocalization of z/k, abbreviation of zaklyuchennyi "prisoner."

zig.x: by 1969, abstracted from the first syllable in zig-zag. Also see zag.

zit.x: "acne pimple," 1966, originally U.S. teenager slang, a word of unknown origin. Related: Zits.

zarf.x:
"holder for a coffee cup," 1836, from Arabic zarf "vessel."
 These holders are usually of metal and of ornamental design in open work. Their immediate object is to prevent the hot cup from burning the fingers. [Century Dictionary, 1891]

zebu.x: Asiatic ox, 1774, from French zebu, ultimately of Tibetan origin. First shown in Europe at the Paris fair of 1752. "[A] name accepted by Buffon from the exhibitors of the animal at a French fair and supposed by him to be an African word." [Century Dictionary]

zest.x: 1670s, from French zeste "piece of orange or lemon peel used as a flavoring," a word of unknown origin. The sense of "thing that adds flavor" is by 1709; that of "keen enjoyment" is attested by 1791 (Boswell, quoting Johnson).

zeta.x: sixth letter of the Greek alphabet, the name attested in English by early 15c; see zed.

Zaire.x: central African nation (1971-1997), from an early alternative name of the Congo River, from Kikongo nzai, dialectal form of nzadi "river." Related: Zairean, Zairese, Zairois.

Zante.x: Ionian island, the ancient Zacynthus, attested by 1610s in reference to wine or other goods from there. The island name is from Greek Zakinthos, which the -nthos suggests is from a lost pre-IE language of Greece. For form evolution, compare currant.

Zeiss.x: in reference to spy-glasses or binoculars, 1905, from the firm founded by German optical instrument manufacturer Carl Zeiss (1816-1888).

Zippo.x: proprietary name of a brand of cigarette lighter, patented 1934 by Zippo Manufacturing Co., Bradford, Pa.

zakat.x: obligatory annual Islamic tax for religious purposes, 1791, from Persian zakat, etc., from Arabic zakah.

zebra.x: African mammal related to the horse and ass, having the body more or less completely striped, c. 1600, from Italian zebra, perhaps via Portuguese, earlier applied to a now-extinct wild ass, a word of uncertain origin, said to be Congolese [OED, 1989], or Amharic [Klein], but perhaps ultimately from Latin equiferus "wild horse," from equus "horse" (see equine) + ferus (see fierce). Related: Zebrine; zebroid.

zeno-.x: late 19c. word-forming element of Greek origin used in reference to the planet Jupiter, from Greek zeno-, combining form from Zeus (see Zeus; also compare Zenobia).

zesty.x: "piquant, agreeably sharp," 1789, from zest + -y (2). Related: Zestily; zestiness.

zilch.x:
"insignificant person," 1933, from use of Zilch as a generic comical-sounding surname for an insignificant person. Probably a nonsense syllable, suggestive of zero and the end of the alphabet (compare zip (n.2)), but Zilch is an actual German surname of Slavic origin.
The popular 1930s satire magazine Ballyhoo from its first issue (August 1931) featured Elmer Zilch and his various and seemingly endless family in its parodies of contemporary advertising and consumer culture. The name became a comedic phrase in U.S.
 "Elmer Zilch" appeared alternately as the hapless victim of aggressive sales pitches and the cynical consumer wise to advertising fakery. His very name yoked the common citizen with the cipher. [Charles F. McGovern, "Sold American," 2006]
The surname had figured by 1931 in journalistic fictional "average person" names; Joe Zilch , a vaudeville performer, and his wife, were regulars in Walter Winchell columns in 1928; Joe Zilch as "average nameless person" is attested by 1921. By the end of 1931, Elmer Zilch was the standard, but Joe continued and Zilch was extended into various unlikely combinations of names meant to represent a fictional average person. More here.
As "nothing, zero" by 1957.
 The [Cadence] agency aims to have each album cover actually promote the record, on the theory that "the day of pretty, boffy, zoomy and zingy covers for the sake of zilch is no more." [Billboard, Oct. 28, 1957]

zippy.x: "full of alacrity, moving rapidly," by 1904, from zip (n.1) in the sense of "energy, force" + -y (2).

zonal.x:
1839, "having the character of a belt or zone," from Late Latin zonalis, from Latin zona (see zone (n.)). With various specific senses in mineralogy, biology, etc.
Zonate (1803) is used in zoology and botany for "marked with rings or bands of color." Zonary (1881, from Latin zonarius) is "having the form of a belt or girdle."

zorro.x: 1838, "South American fox-wolf," from Spanish zorro, masc. of zorra "fox," from Basque azaria "fox." The comic book hero, a variation on Robin Hood set in old Spanish California, was created 1919 by U.S. writer Johnston McCulley (1883-1958). In the New World the word also was applied to neotropical skunks.

zowie.x:
expression of astonishment, by 1911 as a comic-strip word in reaction to something startling.
In 1913 it was a sports-writing and headline vogue word, e.g. "ZOWIE! Kentuckian Gets Divorce Without Wife's Knowledge and Lives For Years With Her, 'Tis Said." [Cincinnati Enquirer, Nov. 11], and Bud Fisher was using it in the Mutt and Jeff strip. On Sept. 4 The Seattle Star ran a brief about a man "arrested while trying to butt down a lamp post" who had told police "One beer makes me think I'm a goat," under the head Two Beers—zowie!

zygo-.x: word-forming element of Greek origin used from 19c. in various scientific words and meaning "yoke," from Greek zygon "yoke," zygoun "to join" (from PIE root *yeug- "to join"). Especially in reference to methods of reproduction.

zymo-.x: before vowels zym-, word-forming element of Greek origin, used from 19c. in scientific and technical terms, from Greek zymē "a leaven," from PIE root *yeue- "to blend, mix food" (see juice (n.)).

Zurich.x: city and lake in Switzerland, German Zürich, said to be ultimately from Celtic root *dur- "water."

zapper.x: electrical pest-killer, 1970, probably an agent-noun from zap in the "kill" sense.

zinger.x: "cruel quip," 1970, from zing in the verbal sense + -er (1). Earlier it was baseball slang for "fastball" (by 1957).

zinnia.x: genus of American herbs of the aster family, 1767, from Modern Latin (Linnæus, 1763), named for German botanist Johann Gottfried Zinn (1729-1759) + abstract noun ending -ia.

zipper.x:
device for binding or locking two edges of fabric, etc., 1925, probably an agent noun from zip (v.1). The trademark taken out on the name that year applied to a boot with zippers, not to the "lightning fastener" itself, which was called a zipper by 1927, also in early use simply zip.
As a verb by 1930, "fasten or seal (a jacket, bag, etc.) with a zipper;" earliest uses often were figurative, slang, in reference to one's mouth.

zither.x: stringed musical instrument, 1850, from German Zither, from Old High German zitara, from Latin cithara, from Greek kithara (see guitar). Sometimes also zithern, zittern.

zouave.x:
1848, soldier in certain French light infantry troops, from French, from Arabic Zwawa, from Berber Igawawaen, name of a Kabyle tribe in Algeria, from which the zouaves originally were recruited in 1831.
The military units soon became exclusively French but served only in Algeria until 1854 and were "distinguished for their dash, intrepidity, and hardihood, and for their peculiar drill and showy Oriental uniform" [Century Dictionary].
Some Northern regiments in the American Civil War adopted the name and elements of the uniform. The women's fashionable zouave jacket (1859) also is based on the uniform.

zounds.x: oath of surprise or anger, c. 1600, altered from (by) God's wounds!, in reference to the wounds of Christ on the Cross. "One of the innumerable oaths having reference to Christ's passion" [Century Dictionary]. Compare gadzooks.

zydeco.x: dance-music genre, by 1949, perhaps (OED, 1989) from Creole French pronunciation of French les haricots "the beans," said to have been part of the title of a popular dance tune ("les haricots sont pas salés").

Zamboni.x: proprietary name of a machine used to resurface ice skating rinks, 1957, trademark of Frank J. Zamboni & Co., Paramount, Calif.

Zebulon.x: masc. proper name, Biblical son of Jacob by Leah, from Hebrew Zebhulun, from zebhul "a dwelling" + diminutive suffix -on. See Genesis xxx.20.

Zenobia.x: fem. proper name, from Greek Zenobia, literally "the force of Zeus," from Zen, collateral form of Zeus, + bia "strength, force," cognate with Sanskrit jya "force, power" (see Jain).

zetetic.x: "investigating, proceeding by inquiry," 1640s, from Modern Latin zeteticus, from Greek zētētikos "searching, inquiring," from zētetos, verbal adjective of zētein "seek for, inquire into." Related: Zetetics; zetetical.

zillion.x:
by 1916, arbitrary humorous coinage with no definite numerical value; a 1922 representation of youthful exaggeration in a magazine story has billion-rillion-zillion years. Compare jillion, gazillion, and see here.
 "They'll be as common as gunnysacks in Oakland in another year, I've been told. They're going to bring 'em over here—zillions of them." [column in Oakland Tribune, Dec. 12, 1916, the topic is Hawaiian melons]

Zenonian.x: 1843, pertaining to one of two Greek thinkers of that name: Zeno of Elea ("Zeno of the Paradoxes," 5c. B.C.E.), who disproved the possibility of motion, by way of Achilles and the tortoise; and Zeno of Citium in Cyprus (c. 300 B.C.E.), founder of stoicism, who taught that the universe was God and was moved by a sort of divine fire.

zaibatsu.x: 1937, "large Japanese capitalist organization, generally based on one family," from Japanese zaibatsu, from zai "wealth" + batzu "clique." In post-WWII use, "cartel, conglomerate business."

zealotry.x: "behavior or feelings of a zealot, excessive or undue zeal, fanaticism," 1650s, from zealot + -ry.

zecchino.x: gold coin of the Venetian republic, 1570s, from Italian (Venetian); see sequin.

zeppelin.x: 1900, from German Zeppelin, short for Zeppelinschiff "Zeppelin ship," after Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin (1838-1917), German general who perfected its design. Compare blimp. Related: Zeppelinous.

ziggurat.x: also zikkurat, 1858, from Assyrian ziqquratu "height, pinnacle," from zaqaru "to be high."

zodiacal.x: "of, pertaining to, or situated in the zodiac," 1570s, from zodiac + -al (1).

zoomancy.x: "divination by observation of animals or their actions," 1888 (Helena Blavatsky), perhaps from earlier zoomantist (1861, Fitzedward Hall, in "Journal of the Asiatic Society" No. III); see zoo- +"animal" -mancy "divination by means of." Related: Zoomantic.

zoonosis.x: "disease communicated to humans by animals" (rabies, etc.), plural zoonoses, 1876, from Greek zōion "animal" (see zoo-) + nosos "disease" (see noso-). Earlier in German, Italian, French.

zoonotic.x: "characteristic of or pertaining to zoonosis," 1878, from zoonosis + -ic.

zoophyte.x: 1620s, literally "animal-plant," Modern Latin, from Greek zōophyton (Aristotle); see zoo- + -phyte. Related: Zoophitic.

zucchini.x: 1915 in English cookery books, 1910 in travel books about Italy as an Italian word (defined as "an odd kind of little squash, very tender and palatable"), from Italian, plural of zucchino, diminutive of zucca "gourd, squash," perhaps from Late Latin cucutia, which is of unknown origin.

Zacchaeus.x: masc. proper name, Biblical, from Late Latin Zacchaeus, from Greek Zakkhaios, from Hebrew zakkay, literally "pure, innocent," from zakhah "was clean, was pure."

Zephaniah.x: masc. proper name, Biblical ninth of the prophets, from Hebrew Tzephanyah "the Lord has hidden."

zymosis.x: "fermentation," 1842, Modern Latin, from Greek zymōsis "fermentation" (see zymo-).

zymotic.x: "pertaining to fermentation," 1842, from Greek zymōtikos, from zymōsis "fermentation" (see zymosis).

zinfandel.x:
"red or white dry California wine," noted by 1870 in California, by 1871 in New Zealand, origin uncertain. The wine is said to have been known in U.S. since 1829.
Some wine experts suggest a corruption of the Austrian grape name Zierfandler, though these grapes are not related to those of zinfandel. According to a now-extinct internet article (formerly at http://ww3.stratsplace.com/):
 The similarity in the names Zinfandel and Zierfandler arouses some speculation. Modern vine identification systems did not yet exist in 1829, so it is conceivable that the cuttings George Gibbs imported to the USA had never been correctly identified in Austria.

zirconium.x: metallic chemical element, 1808, coined in Modern Latin by German chemist and mineralogist Martin Heinrich Klaproth (1743-1817) in 1789; so called because it was obtained from zircon. With-ium, name-ending of metallic elements.

zoologist.x: "biologist, one versed in zoology," 1660s, from zoology + -ist. Also zoologer (1660s).

zoomorphic.x:
"representative of animals," 1845, from zoo- "animal" + -morphic "of or pertaining to form," from Greek morphē "shape," a word of uncertain etymology.
Originally in paleography, of letters in old manuscripts formed of strangely contorted figures of animals, and correlated with anthropomorphic. Later especially "representative of a god in the form of an animal." Related: Zoomorphism "attribution of animal form to a deity" (1822, by 1796 in German); zoomorphy.

zoophagous.x: "carnivorous, eating animals," 1788, from zoo- "animal" + -phagous "eating." Related: Zoophagy; zoophage.

zygodactyl.x: "having the toes arranged in pairs" (two before and two behind, as certain birds have them), etymologically "yoke-toed;" 1828, Modern Latin, from Greek zygon "yoke" (from PIE root *yeug- "to join") + daktylos "toe" (see dactyl).

Zarathustra.x: from Avestan Zarathushtra (see Zoroastrian). Related: Zarathustrian; Zarathustrianism.

zooxanthella.x: plural zooxanthellae, yellow pigmentary particles found in nature, 1889, from German (Brandt, 1881), from Greek zōion "animal" (from PIE root *gwei- "to live") + xanthos "yellow" (see xantho-) + Latin suffix -ella.
